the question of how far a single, simple model can be applied to different tasks of nonliteral language classification, in different languages, and at different granularites.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a simple LSTM is able to achieve good performance on a variety of tasks of non literal classification, while the choice of embeddings is crucial for the performance.
a simple context encoding model performs well for non literal language detection, especially in German, but that the choice of embeddings is crucial.
a simple LSTM model is a strong baseline for non literal language detection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a simple LSTM can perform well on non literal language detection at both the token and construction levels, and that the choice of embeddings is task and genre dependent.
there is no single best approach to non literal language classification, and that the performance of different models varies according to language, granularity, and genre.
there is not a one-size-fits-all approach to non literal language classification.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the same simple model can be used for different tasks, and that the performance of word embeddings is highly dependent on the genre.
the proposed model is able to outperform the state of the arts in two tasks and that the model is able to generalize well to new tasks.
the same model can be used to tackle multiple non literal language tasks in different languages, and it outperforms state of the art results on some of the tasks.
